title: Speculative Execution
summary: Executing past uncertain points before they resolve, how rollback works when the guess is wrong, and the security lesson Spectre taught the industry.

slides.markdown:
**Speculation** means executing instructions past a point whose outcome isn't known yet — usually a branch, sometimes a memory access whose true dependence isn't confirmed. Rather than stalling until the uncertainty resolves, the core guesses (via branch prediction, [branch-prediction](branch-prediction)) and keeps executing down that path.

This pays off because prediction is usually right — modern predictors exceed 95% accuracy on typical code, so most speculative work turns out to be exactly the work the program needed, just started earlier than a conservative in-order machine ever could.

slides.sectionTitle: Nothing is real until it commits
slides.markdown:
The core rule that makes speculation safe: speculative results stay invisible to architectural state — registers, memory — until the instruction **commits** ([out-of-order-execution](out-of-order-execution)'s reorder buffer), which only happens once the uncertain point (the branch) is confirmed correct.

Until then, a speculative result lives only in temporary hardware structures — reservation stations, the ROB — that can simply be discarded if the guess turns out wrong. This is what lets the hardware speculate aggressively without ever risking incorrect program behavior becoming visible.

![A misprediction rolling back speculative state via the reorder buffer and a saved checkpoint of the register map](assets/speculation-rollback.svg)

When a branch resolves against its prediction, the core discards every younger, still-speculative instruction in the ROB, restores the register-rename map to the branch's checkpoint, and redirects fetch to the correct path — none of the wrong-path work ever touched visible state.

assets.alt: A misprediction rolling back speculative state via the reorder buffer and a saved checkpoint of the register map

slides.markdown:
Branches aren't the only speculation point. A **load** can execute speculatively before an earlier **store**'s address is known, betting the store won't write the same address (won't "alias"). If wrong, the load's result and anything that consumed it must be squashed and re-executed, like a branch misprediction.

This matters because waiting for every earlier store's address before issuing a load would stall memory-heavy code badly; store-to-load speculation recovers most of that time, at the cost of occasional rollbacks.

The rollback story is clean — but not the whole story. Speculative instructions can leave **microarchitectural side effects**, especially cache state, even after the ROB discards their results. A squashed load can still pull data into cache; later code measures cache-hit timing to infer *what* was loaded.

This is the root of **Spectre-class attacks**: leaking data through a timing channel rollback never touches. Architectural correctness alone was never enough; timing side channels are now a first-class concern (brief mention only — see Security → appsec).

slides.sectionTitle: Speculation depth: how far is too far
slides.markdown:
Speculation isn't limited to one guess at a time — a wide, deep OoO core routinely speculates past **multiple** unresolved branches simultaneously, each one adding another layer of "might get thrown away." Real cores track this with a **checkpoint per in-flight branch**: a snapshot of the register-rename map table taken at the branch, cheap enough to take dozens of times per cycle window.

If branch B2 (deeper in the pipeline than B1) mispredicts, the core restores the checkpoint taken at B2 and discards everything issued after it — B1's correct prediction and any work speculated past it is untouched. If B1 turns out to have mispredicted instead, everything after B1 — including all the speculative work done "under" B2 — is thrown away regardless of whether B2's own guess was right.

The number of checkpoints a core can hold (commonly single digits to ~16 in real designs) directly caps how many unresolved branches can be in flight before the core must stall fetch — another concrete limit alongside ROB size and issue width.

slides.sectionTitle: When speculation itself is the hazard
slides.markdown:
Not all speculation is about branch direction. **Speculative memory disambiguation** (see register-renaming) guesses a load doesn't alias an earlier store and lets it race ahead; **value speculation** on some designs predicts a load's *value* before it even reaches memory. Both follow the same contract as branch speculation: execute optimistically, keep results non-architectural until confirmed, and replay (not just squash) if the guess was wrong.

Replay is more expensive than a branch flush because it's often narrower — instead of discarding everything after a point, the pipeline re-issues just the dependent instructions that consumed the bad guess, which requires tracking a dependence chain rather than a simple age cutoff.

This generalization — "guess, execute non-committally, verify, recover" — is the single mechanism underlying branch prediction, memory disambiguation, and (as the next slide covers) the side-channel risk that comes with doing all of this on shared hardware.

slides.sectionTitle: Meltdown: when speculation crosses a permission boundary
slides.markdown:
Spectre (the prior slide) tricks a victim's *own* correctly-permissioned code into speculatively touching data it wouldn't normally access. **Meltdown** (2018, mostly Intel) is a distinct bug: the CPU speculatively executed a load **before checking the page table's permission bit**, so user code could issue a load to a kernel-only address, and the CPU would fetch the value into the cache before the (too-late) permission fault rolled the instruction back architecturally.

The data itself never reached a register the program could read directly — but the cache line it landed in did, and that's enough: a follow-up load to an address that depends on the secret byte (the classic Spectre-style cache-timing probe) reveals the byte through timing, one bit at a time, entirely bypassing the permission check that should have stopped it.

Meltdown's fix (KPTI — kernel page-table isolation) unmapped the kernel's address space from user page tables almost entirely, forcing a TLB flush on every syscall/interrupt — a real, measured 5–30% throughput tax on syscall-heavy workloads, and a clean example of a security fix landing squarely on the performance side of the ledger.

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: the cost of getting speculation right vs wrong
slides.markdown:
Speculation only pays off if it's usually right, so the economics matter. A correctly-speculated branch costs essentially nothing extra — the work would have happened eventually anyway. A **mispredicted** one costs the full pipeline-flush penalty (15-20+ cycles on a deep modern pipeline, per branch-prediction's numbers slide) *plus* the wasted execution-unit cycles spent on instructions that never should have run.

At a typical ~90-95% real-world prediction accuracy and one branch every 5-6 instructions, the expected cost per instruction is small (well under half a cycle) — which is exactly why the industry kept pushing speculation more aggressively for two decades: the *average* case is nearly free, even though the worst case is expensive.

Mitigations for the Spectre/Meltdown class of bugs (retpolines, speculative store bypass disable, KPTI) each claw back some of that average-case gain in exchange for closing a specific side channel — which is why disabling them wholesale is tempting for performance but a real security regression, and why modern kernels expose them as tunable, workload-dependent trade-offs rather than always-on.
